The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-12T12:24:00Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-12T12:24:02Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-12T12:17:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-12T12:25:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 2 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T12:26:04Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 17.7% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 24.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 16.7% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 0.9833333333333333% {series_before} before it began, 17.6875% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 24.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 3,022.30 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

What Code-Fix read in the source, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran to check it, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] Yes. Old replicas crash on '2400/8 {F1.1}' because something writes `str(SummaryEntry)` under the bare shopper id, which is where revision 5470c1a reads. That writer isn't in this repository: the cache is reached only through a `LookUpSummary` seam the deployment supplies, and no code here writes entries. My patch only moves where this revision reads, to `summary_key_for(shopper_id)` = `summary:v2:<shopper_id>`. On its own, that leaves the new-format text under the bare key and the old replicas still failing on it. For the change to help, the writer outside this repo must store new-format entries under `summary_key_for(shopper_id)` and never under the bare shopper id. It must also stop writing that shape at the old address while any 5470c1a replica is still serving. Any '/'-format entries already sitting under bare shopper ids need deleting or expiring before the rollout resumes.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The new revision changed what a summary cache entry holds. It used to be a bare cents figure and is now 'amount/items' text (`_ENTRY_FORMAT`). The replicas still running the earlier revision read those same entries and raised ValueError on the new text in src/io_shop/summary_cache.py instead of treating it as a miss, so the account page request failed.
cause_in_plain_words: A software update changed the format of a saved summary of each shopper's spending, and the older version, still running beside the new one because the update stopped partway, could not read the new format and failed the account page.
still_at_risk: Account pages could fail again if revision 696c33a goes out again while the earlier revision is still serving, or if cache entries in its new format are left where the earlier revision reads.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service's share of failed requests rose well above its usual level. (cites AL1; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: The failing account page requests raised ValueError when they read a summary cache entry, '{G3714.1}', that was not a figure in cents, in src/io_shop/summary_cache.py. (cites G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc956, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: The cache held entries in the new 'amount/items' text format that revision 696c33a introduced, and the replicas reading them expected a bare cents figure. The new revision's own reader returns no error on text it cannot read, so the error comes from the reader in the earlier revision. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; Gc956, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 4: Deploy P2 at {P2.1} rolled out revision 696c33a, which brought in the new entry format. As of {T10.1}, its rolling update was paused partway, with replicas on 696c33a and on 5470c1a both serving against the same cache. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; T10, under "What Argus did, in order"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed")
causal_chain 4 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy P1 of revision 5470c1a: the service was measured healthy with it in place. The metrics read before the onset showed the usual error rate, account pages rendered normally before the onset, and the service returned to normal after the confirmed rollback left 5470c1a running. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gad41, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; M1, under "Actions it took"; T21, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 5: The new revision changed the format of cache entries that the still-serving older replicas also read, and the older revision's reader raised an error on the new format instead of treating it as a miss. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc956, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen, before the change went out, that the revision already serving could read cache entries in the new revision's format.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The format mismatch would have been caught before deploy P2, and the account pages would not have failed.
contributing_factors 2: No automatic rollout analysis was seen that halted or reverted io-shop's rolling update when its error rate rose. The rollout stayed partway, with both revisions serving.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The mixed-revision state would have been reverted soon after the error rate rose, which would have shortened the failure.
contributing_factors 3: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been brought in as soon as the alert fired, instead of the response depending on automation alone.
action_items 1: Add a pre-deploy check, for every change to the format of a cached or stored entry, that runs the serving revision's reader against entries written in the candidate revision's format.
action_items 2: Add automated rollout analysis to io-shop's rolling updates that halts and reverts the rollout when the error rate rises while revisions are mixed.
action_items 3: Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page.
went_well 5: Code-Fix wrote a fix and said plainly that it helps only together with a change outside the repository, so no partial fix was kept.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged, and whether a went_wrong item is one its field excludes.
